newsitem.title: USA: Democrats to press for end to physician gag rule.
newsitem.headline: Democrats to press for end to physician gag rule.

text.p: Key Democratic senators charged Thursday that Republican leaders unfairly blocked debate on a plan to end "gag rules" imposed on physicians by insurers, and pledged to press repeatedly for a vote on the plan.

The fight delayed Senate action on a $23 billion fiscal 1997 appropriations bill covering the Treasury Department and the White House. Finally, late Thursday after 25 hours of debate, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott pulled the appropriations bill from the Senate floor.
"What they are effectively doing is gagging the U.S. Senate by denying a vote," said Sen. Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts.

Kennedy and Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon said they believed the Senate, if given a chance, would vote to give doctors the right to discuss all available medical treatments with their patients and would bar health plans from imposing so-called "gag rules."
"What these (health) plans are doing is leaving patients in the dark," Wyden told reporters.

Wyden told reporters his tactic will be to offer it to all other legislation brought before the Senate and he felt Republicans were leaning toward supporting it as a pro-consumer measure. He said he would expect at least 52 votes for passage.
"We are going to look at every single train that is moving through," he said after Lott halted the debate.

The Treasury bill is one of nine remaining money bills Congress must pass before it adjourns for the year at the end of the month. Unfinished spending bills will likely be wrapped into one massive spending bill to fund the government for the fiscal year starting 1997.

Republican senators tried to substitute a resolution calling for a study of the physician gag rule problem, but Wyden and Kennedy said that was not enough. "We think to do nothing puts patients at risk," Wyden said.
Under Wyden's amendment, doctors would be free to tell patients when a treatment was available for their condition that was not covered by their health plan.

However, it would not overturn what are called "anti-disparagement clauses" in contracts. Doctors would not have blanket permission to suggest a patient join another plan that provided better coverage and they could not run down the health plan for which they work.

Republican leaders used a procedural move to block a vote on the gag rule amendment Wednesday. Wyden won a majority 51-48 votes but needed 60 votes to clear the procedural roadblock. He said the majority vote gave him confidence it would pass if a straight up-or-down vote were held.

The amendment is supported by most medical organisations. The umbrella trade association for managed health care, the American Association of Health Plans, told Congress the anti-gag rule was unnecessary because no such rules exist.

"We have not found any examples where this has actually happened," AAHP spokesman Donald White said in a telephone interview. "No one should be in a plan that limits communications by physicians on treatment options," he said.

The AAHP has testified before Congress in support of open communications between doctors and patients on medical care, but warns that doctors should not be able to denigrate the health plan to which they belong. About one-sixth of health plans have rules prohibiting disparagement, the AAHP said.
